verifiedClaims.note: § 40-6-123(a): no person shall 'turn a vehicle from a direct course or change lanes or move right or left upon a roadway unless and until such movement can be made with reasonable safety. No person shall so turn any vehicle without giving an appropriate and timely signal'. Accurate as a general statement; the 'when required' qualifier is handled in the turn-only-lane claim below.

verifiedClaims.claim: Under Georgia state law, there are specific times when drivers are required to signal: Making a turn at an intersection; Turning out of a private or commercial driveway or entrance; When changing lanes or merging into traffic; When entering traffic from a parallel parking space; In preparation for passing other vehicles
verifiedClaims.currentValue: O.C.G.A. § 40-6-123(a) requires a signal before turning at an intersection, turning 'to enter a private road or driveway', or otherwise turning 'from a direct course', changing lanes or moving 'right or left upon a roadway' (which covers pulling out of a driveway onto the road, merging and moving over to pass); § 40-6-123(d) extends the signal lamps to an intention to 'start from a parked position'; and § 40-6-123(c) — which the list omits — requires a signal before stopping or suddenly decreasing speed 'when there is an opportunity to give such signal'. In every case the signal is required only when another driver could be affected: § 40-6-123(b) says 'when required' and Georgia courts read that to mean the signal is owed to the drivers behind you and those approaching from the opposite direction.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 40-6-123(a)-(d); Bowers v. State, 221 Ga. App. 886 (1996); Morgan v. State, 309 Ga. App. 923 (2011)
verifiedClaims.note: The list is a fair paraphrase but three details are off: the statute names turning INTO a private road or driveway (pulling out is covered by the general 'move right or left upon a roadway' language, not by a driveway clause); 'passing' is not named — it is a lane change; and the stop/slow-down signal in subsection (c) is missing, which matters for the 'slamming on your brakes' bullet later. Suggested list: turning at an intersection; turning into (or out onto the road from) a private road or driveway; changing lanes or moving right or left, including to pass or merge; starting from a parked position; stopping or suddenly slowing when there is a chance to signal. Add '(O.C.G.A. § 40-6-123)'.

verifiedClaims.claim: Right turns must be made from the far-right lane, unless multiple lanes are appropriately marked as “right-turn only” lanes.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: O.C.G.A. § 40-6-120(1): 'Both the approach for a right turn and a right turn shall be made as close as practicable to the right-hand curb or edge of the roadway.' The section (rewritten by HB 1231, effective July 1, 2010) contains no marked-lane exception for right turns; where a second right-turn lane is marked, the duty to follow it comes from § 40-6-20(a) (drivers 'shall obey the instructions of an official traffic-control device').
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 40-6-120(1) (2025 Code of Georgia, via Justia); O.C.G.A. § 40-6-20(a) (reused from facts-2586)
verifiedClaims.note: Substance is right; the exception is real in practice but rests on the traffic-control-device statute, not on § 40-6-120. Add the pinpoint '(O.C.G.A. § 40-6-120)'.

verifiedClaims.claim: They cannot turn left from a center lane as it would cause them to cross in front of other traffic. They must turn from the far-left lane or from lanes that are specifically marked as left-turning lanes.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: O.C.G.A. § 40-6-120(2)(B): the driver 'shall approach the turn in the extreme left-hand lane lawfully available to traffic moving in the direction of travel of the turning vehicle'; (2)(C): with multiple left-turn lanes the driver 'shall exit the intersection in the same relative travel lane as the vehicle entered' and 'shall not be permitted to make a lane change once the intersection has been entered'. On a road with a two-way center turn lane the left turn is made FROM that center lane: § 40-6-126 allows a vehicle into the central lane only 'for the purpose of making a left turn' and for no more than 300 feet.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 40-6-120(2)(A)-(C); O.C.G.A. § 40-6-126 (2025 Code of Georgia, via Justia)
verifiedClaims.note: 'Cannot turn left from a center lane' is wrong for Abercorn-style roads with a center turn lane, where the center lane is the only lawful place to turn left from. Reword to 'from a middle through lane' and, optionally, add the § 40-6-126 center-turn-lane rule and the § 40-6-120(2)(C) no-lane-change-in-the-intersection rule for double left-turn lanes.

verifiedClaims.claim: Drivers behind you will know that you intend to turn left or turn right. However, it may not be a good idea to assume that traffic coming from in front of you or from other directions know that. Signaling is just a good habit to engage in and an easy way to help prevent a crash.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Georgia law answers this directly. Because § 40-6-123(b) requires a signal only 'when required' — that is, when it is needed to alert a driver behind you or one approaching from the opposite direction — the Court of Appeals held in State v. Goodman, 220 Ga. App. 169 (1996) that a left-turn signal 'was not necessary' from a left-turn-only lane where the driver's 'sole legal option was a left turn' and no other traffic was affected. But the same courts hold that a driver 'may [be pulled] over for failing to signal when traffic conditions require the use of such signal' (Morgan v. State, 309 Ga. App. 923 (2011)), so if oncoming or following drivers could be affected, the signal is still required — and in a crash case the other driver will argue it was.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: State v. Goodman, 220 Ga. App. 169, 469 S.E.2d 327 (Ga. Ct. App. 1996) (Beasley, C.J., and Pope, P.J., concurring — binding precedent); Morgan v. State, 309 Ga. App. 923 (Ga. Ct. App. 2011); Bowers v. State, 221 Ga. App. 886 (1996) (physical precedent only)
verifiedClaims.note: The H2 asks a legal question and the answer gives none. Goodman verbatim: 'the statute contemplates instances in which a turn on a roadway can be made with reasonable safety without the use of a turn signal, i.e., where a signal is not necessary to alert other drivers of a motorist's intention to turn ... Therefore, a left turn signal was not necessary, and there was no violation of OCGA § 40-6-123'. Morgan notes Bowers and Clark are 'not concurred in by all panel members' and so 'do not constitute binding precedent', but Goodman was unanimous and Morgan itself restates the rule. Keep the good-habit advice after the law. Do NOT cite the Washington, Vermont or Texas turn-only-lane cases — different statutes (their 100-foot rule is not Georgia's).

verifiedClaims.claim: Under Georgia law, there is no specific time or distance stated. However, the law requires you to signal continuously for a sufficient amount of time. Paraphrased, you must signal long enough to give drivers behind you or around you sufficient notice.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 40-6-123(b) (2025 Code of Georgia, via Justia)
verifiedClaims.note: Correct. Verbatim: 'A signal of intention to turn right or left or change lanes when required shall be given continuously for a time sufficient to alert the driver of a vehicle proceeding from the rear in the same direction or a driver of a vehicle approaching from the opposite direction.' Georgia has no 100-foot rule — that language belongs to the Uniform Vehicle Code and to states such as Washington (RCW 46.61.305), Vermont and Texas; do not add it. Optional precision: the statute names drivers behind you and drivers coming toward you, not 'around you'. Add '(O.C.G.A. § 40-6-123)'.

verifiedClaims.claim: Turning on your signal at the same time you change lanes; Signaling seconds before you turn; Slamming on your brakes and then signaling, such as when almost missing an exit; Darting in and out of lanes while signaling
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 40-6-123(a) ('appropriate and timely signal'), (b) ('continuously for a time sufficient'), (c) (signal before stopping or 'suddenly decreas[ing] the speed')
verifiedClaims.note: Illustrative and consistent with the statute; the brakes bullet maps to subsection (c), which is why the earlier list should mention stopping/slowing.

verifiedClaims.claim: While often, the liable party may be the driver who failed to signal, the law will never assume that. An investigation into the cause of every crash must occur, so that the appropriate party can be held liable for the damages.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: While the driver who failed to signal is often the liable party, the law does not assume it: fault has to be proven from the evidence of what each driver did, and a rule-of-the-road violation is negligence per se but not liability per se.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Perkins v. Kranz, 316 Ga. App. 171 (2012), quoting Yasinsac v. Colonial Oil Properties, 246 Ga. App. 484 (2000) ('negligence per se is not liability per se') — reused from facts-2586; Central Anesthesia Associates v. Worthy, 254 Ga. 728 (1985) — reused from facts-1740
verifiedClaims.note: 'An investigation ... must occur' states a legal requirement that does not exist; what is true is that the injured person carries the burden of proof. Wording change only.

verifiedClaims.claim: The driver who did not use a turn signal before turning or changing lanes is typically considered at fault. Georgia law requires drivers to signal their intentions before turning or changing lanes.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: The driver who did not signal before turning or changing lanes is typically considered at fault. O.C.G.A. § 40-6-123 requires drivers to signal before turning or changing lanes whenever another driver could be affected, and violating a rule of the road is negligence per se in Georgia — it establishes the driver's duty and the breach of it, leaving the injured person to prove that the failure caused the crash and what the damages are.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 40-6-123(a)-(b); O.C.G.A. § 51-1-6; Central Anesthesia Associates, P.C. v. Worthy, 254 Ga. 728 (1985) ('negligence per se supplies only the duty and breach of duty elements'); § 40-6-123 annotations (Harrison v. Jenkins, 235 Ga. App. 665; Folds v. Auto Mut. Indem. Co., 55 Ga. App. 198 (1937))
verifiedClaims.note: Nothing false; the section is the natural place to name the statute and the negligence-per-se doctrine, which faq:1 already relies on. Central Anesthesia is reused from facts-1740; the Justia annotations under § 40-6-123 record negligence per se for a stop without signal lights (Harrison) and, under the predecessor section, for failure to give the required signal (Folds).

verifiedClaims.claim: Drivers have a legal duty of care to avoid causing harm to others. This includes properly signaling to help ensure the safety of all road users.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 40-6-241(b) ('A driver shall exercise due care in operating a motor vehicle on the highways of this state') — reused from facts-2586; O.C.G.A. § 40-6-123

verifiedClaims.claim: While the driver who failed to signal is usually at fault, other drivers involved in the accident might share liability. However, this is only if the other party’s negligence contributed to the crash in some way.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33(b) (trier of fact apportions damages 'among the persons who are liable according to the percentage of fault of each person')
verifiedClaims.note: The speeding-through-an-intersection example that follows is illustrative. Reused from facts-1740 / facts-2586.

verifiedClaims.claim: In this situation, the driver's employer might be held liable under a legal doctrine called, “respondeat superior.” This doctrine holds employers responsible for things their employees did if those actions occurred within the scope of their employment.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 51-2-2 (2025 Code of Georgia, via Justia): 'Every person shall be liable for torts committed by his wife, his child, or his servant by his command or in the prosecution and within the scope of his business, whether the same are committed by negligence or voluntarily.'
verifiedClaims.note: Accurate. Optional: add '(O.C.G.A. § 51-2-2)'. Note the section lives at title-51/chapter-2/ with no article segment on Justia.

verifiedClaims.claim: In some cases, the owner of the vehicle (if different from the driver) may be liable. This is especially true if they knowingly allowed an unsafe or unlicensed driver to use their vehicle.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Gunn v. Booker, 259 Ga. 343, 381 S.E.2d 286 (Ga. 1989) (negligent entrustment: liable if the owner entrusts the vehicle 'with actual knowledge that the person ... is incompetent by reason of his age or inexperience, or his physical or mental condition, or his known habit of recklessness'); O.C.G.A. § 40-5-122 ('No person shall knowingly authorize or permit a motor vehicle owned by him or under his control to be driven upon any highway by any person who is not authorized under this chapter or who is not licensed')
verifiedClaims.note: 'Knowingly' is the load-bearing word and the post has it: Georgia requires the owner's ACTUAL knowledge of the driver's incompetence, and per Schofield v. Hertz Corp. (Ga. Ct. App. 1991) an owner's failure to check for a licence 'is of no consequence' unless the driver was also negligent. Optional: name the doctrine ('negligent entrustment') and, for a family car, the family purpose doctrine (Danforth v. Bulman, Ga. Ct. App. 2005).

verifiedClaims.claim: Georgia follows a modified comparative negligence rule. What this means for drivers is that fault for any crash can be shared among multiple parties. The percentage of fault is based on each party’s assessed degree of responsibility.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33(a), (b) — reused from facts-1740 / facts-2586; matches the writer-profile jurisdiction table
verifiedClaims.note: Internal link returns 200. Optional: add '(O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33)' in the body to match faq:3, which already cites it.

verifiedClaims.claim: The bottom line is this: as long as the injured victim is less than 50 percent at fault, a claim for compensation is still possible. That said, any compensation awarded to a partially liable victim will be reduced by his or her percentage of fault.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33(g) ('the plaintiff shall not be entitled to receive any damages if the plaintiff is 50 percent or more responsible'); (a) (damages reduced 'in proportion to his or her percentage of fault')

verifiedClaims.claim: Independent witnesses, dashcam or nearby camera footage, and the police report are the usual routes, since a signal leaves no physical trace after the crash. Identifying witnesses at the scene is what makes this provable.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Independent witnesses, dashcam or nearby camera footage, and the police report are the usual routes, since a signal rarely leaves physical evidence — though in a serious crash a reconstruction expert can sometimes examine the turn-signal bulb's filament, which deforms differently depending on whether the lamp was lit at impact. Identifying witnesses at the scene is what makes this provable.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: SAE Technical Paper 2013-01-0752 (Przybyla, Rush, Melcher & Robinson, 'Light Bulb Filament Distortion Thresholds by Voltage and Delta-V', April 2013) — abstract: 'Through examination of bulb filaments for hot or cold shock, accident reconstruction professionals can gain information about which bulbs were and were not illuminated prior to the collision.'
verifiedClaims.note: Renders into FAQPage structured data. 'Leaves no physical trace' is an absolute that crash reconstruction contradicts: lamp-filament (hot-shock / cold-shock) analysis is an established SAE-documented technique for determining whether a lamp was lit at impact. Soften rather than expand; the practical advice in the answer is sound. On the police report: no Georgia primary source was located on the admissibility of the officer's opinion of fault (facts-1740 reached the same result), so leave the report described as an investigative route, not as proof.

statuteCitations.name: Turning movements; signals required on turning, changing lanes, slowing, or stopping — (a) no turn, lane change or move right/left without 'an appropriate and timely signal' when it can be made with reasonable safety; (b) signal 'when required' given 'continuously for a time sufficient to alert' the driver behind or one approaching from the opposite direction (no distance rule); (c) signal before stopping or suddenly slowing; (d) signal lamps also for starting from a parked position, and never as a 'do pass' courtesy

Methods of turning at intersections (rewritten by HB 1231, eff. July 1, 2010) — (1) right turn as close as practicable to the right-hand curb or edge; (2)(B) left turn from the extreme left-hand lane lawfully available; (2)(C) multiple left-turn lanes: exit in the same relative lane, no lane change once in the intersection
U-turns — prohibited on a curve, near the crest of a grade where the vehicle cannot be seen, where the turn cannot be made in safety without interfering with other traffic, or where posted

Starting parked vehicle — 'No person shall start a vehicle which is stopped, standing, or parked unless and until such movement can be made with reasonable safety' (the signal requirement for starting from a parked position is in § 40-6-123(d), not here)

Signals by hand and arm or signal lights — (a) either method; (b) signal lights mandatory where the steering post is more than 24 inches from the left body limit or more than 14 feet from the rear limit
Method of giving hand and arm signals — from the left side: left turn horizontal, right turn upward, stop or decrease speed downward
Central lane for turning — a two-way center lane may be entered only to make a left turn, not more than 300 feet before the turn, and not driven in for more than 300 feet
Violations of Chapter 6 (Uniform Rules of the Road) are misdemeanors unless otherwise declared
Obedience to traffic-control devices required (a) — basis for following a marked second turn lane (reused from facts-2586)
Distracted driving — (b) 'A driver shall exercise due care in operating a motor vehicle' (reused from facts-2586)

Permitting unlicensed person to drive — 'No person shall knowingly authorize or permit a motor vehicle owned by him or under his control to be driven upon any highway by any person who is not authorized under this chapter or who is not licensed'

Liability for torts of spouse, child, or servant — respondeat superior: 'Every person shall be liable for torts committed by ... his servant by his command or in the prosecution and within the scope of his business' (Justia path has no article segment)
Recovery for breach of a legal duty — statutory basis of negligence per se (reused from facts-1740 / facts-2586)
Apportionment of damages — (a) reduction by plaintiff's percentage of fault; (b) apportionment among persons liable; (g) plaintiff barred at 50 percent or more (reused from facts-1740 / facts-2586)
Injuries to the person — two-year limitation (reused from facts-1740; not stated in this post)

Morgan v. State, 309 Ga. App. 923 (Ga. Ct. App. June 2, 2011) — 'a turn signal is not required if changing lanes [or making a turn] without a signal is reasonably safe' but 'an officer may pull over a motorist for failing to signal when traffic conditions require the use of such signal'; notes Bowers and Clark are not binding precedent
